extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, and students of poetics/dramatic composition
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance for composing tragic drama (plot, character, recognition, diction, and staging) based on Aristotle's Poetics. Focuses on how incidents should be constructed, types of recognition, character requirements, and language/metrical considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causality and unity of the plot (no external Machinery)
rubrics_metrics.description: The travelling/complication of the plot, no less than the complication, must be brought about by the plot itself, and not by Machinery,—as in the Medea, or in the Return of the Greeks in the Iliad. Machinery should be employed only for events external to the drama,—either such as are previous to it and outside the sphere of human knowledge, or subsequent to it and which need to be foretold and announced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure every incident within the action arises from internal, plausible causes of the plot itself. Use gods, oracular statements, or contrivances only for matters outside the action or before/after the drama. Avoid deus ex machina that resolves conflicts inside the drama; irrational occurrences within the action offend the spectator (example: the irrationality in Sophocles' Oedipus must be handled as outside the drama's internal causation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and nature of recognition (ranking of possibilities)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are only certain ways recognition can occur: the incident may be outside the drama proper; it may fall within the action of the play; or someone may be about to do an irreparable deed and make the discovery before it is done. Of these ways, to be about to act knowing the consequences and then not to act is the worst (shocking but not tragic). Better is that the deed should be perpetrated; better still, that it should be perpetrated in ignorance and the discovery made afterwards; the best is recognition occurring in the very act (e.g., Cresphontes, Merope sparing her son; Iphigenia recognising her brother just in time).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer recognitions that occur at a decisive moment within the action and produce a startling but probable effect. Avoid scenarios where a character intends a wicked deed knowingly and abstains—this shocks without producing true tragedy. Rank possible recognition-timings and choose the one that produces the strongest tragic effect consistent with probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of recognition and their artistic merit
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition (anagnorisis) occurs in several kinds: (1) by signs/tokens (congenital marks, scars, necklaces) — the least artistic; (2) by devices invented at will by the poet — inartistic; (3) by recollection/memory when seeing or hearing something; (4) by process of reasoning. The best recognition is that which arises from the incidents themselves and by probable means (as in Oedipus, Iphigenia).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid recognitions that depend on arbitrary tokens or on the poet having a character speak to reveal identity (poet-invented solutions). Favor recognitions that follow naturally from events and are probable, especially those that the plot itself warrants. Use memory or reasoning-based recognitions when they naturally fit the situation; tokens are permissible but less artistic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character: four aims (goodness, propriety, verisimilitude, consistency)
rubrics_metrics.description: In respect of Character there are four things to be aimed at. First, and most important, it must be good — any speech or action manifesting a moral purpose shows character and the purpose being good makes character good. Second is propriety: certain traits suit certain sexes/roles (e.g., manly valour is inappropriate for a woman). Third is that character must be true to life (distinct from goodness and propriety). Fourth is consistency: even if an original character is inconsistent, he must be consistently inconsistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design characters whose purposes are morally intelligible and whose traits are appropriate to their social/sexual/age roles. Ensure realism—characters should act in ways a viewer would find credible—and maintain internal consistency (if a character is capricious, display that caprice consistently). Examples of violations: Menelaus in Orestes (needlessly bad), Odysseus' lament (incongruous), Iphigenia at Aulis (inconsistent portrayal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Action and character must follow necessity or probability
rubrics_metrics.description: As in plot construction, so too in character portrayal, the poet should always aim either at the necessary or the probable. A person of a given character should speak or act in a given way, by the rule either of necessity or of probability; just as one event should follow another by necessary or probable sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When planning incidents and dialogue, ensure actions and utterances are dictated by plausible character motives or by inevitable causal chain. Avoid arbitrary behaviour or sequences that violate audience expectations of necessity/probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation: ennoble while preserving likeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Since Tragedy is an imitation of persons who are above the common level, the example of good portrait‑painters should be followed. They reproduce the distinctive form of the original but make a likeness which is true to life and yet more beautiful. So too the poet should, in representing men quick or slow to anger, preserve the type and yet ennoble it (e.g., Achilles as portrayed by Agathon and Homer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model characters on recognizable human types but elevate language/action to give them grandeur. Keep the essential traits that make the type recognizable, but refine and idealize for poetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance and brevity of episodes in drama
rubrics_metrics.description: After the names being once assumed, it remains to fill in the episodes. We must see that they are relevant to the action. In a drama, the episodes are short, the epic poem uses episodes to extend the narrative. The Odyssey’s many episodes are appropriate to epic length but in drama episodes should be brief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include only episodes that directly serve the plot’s complication or unravelling; keep them concise. Avoid sprawling episodic expansion characteristic of epic within the drama, which diffuses tragic intensity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division into Complication and Unravelling (peripeteia and denouement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every tragedy falls into two parts—Complication and Unravelling or Dénouement. By the Complication is meant all that comes between the beginning of the action and the part which marks the turning point from bad fortune to good (or vice versa). The Unravelling is that which comes between the beginning of the change and the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure the play so the turning point (peripeteia) is clearly defined and the subsequent unravelling follows logically and completely to the end. Ensure the Complication organically leads to the change of fortune and the Unravelling resolves consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of Tragedy and balancing merits
rubrics_metrics.description: There are four kinds of Tragedy: the Complicated (depending on reversal and recognition), the Simple, the Pathetic (motive = passion), and the Ethical (motive = moral character). The poet should endeavour, if possible, to combine all poetic merits, or at least the greatest number and most important ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide which type your play chiefly belongs to and try to secure the most significant merits for that kind. Balance reversal, recognition, passionate motive, and ethical depth according to your aims; be wary of trying to do too much poorly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Epic structure / multiplicity of plots
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not make a Tragedy into an Epic structure; by that is meant one with a multiplicity of plots. In the Epic poem, owing to its length, each part assumes its proper magnitude; in the drama the result is far from the expectation. Poets who dramatise an entire epic tale often fail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a single, coherent portion of a larger story to dramatize. Avoid attempting the whole sweep of a long epic in one play; prioritize unity and depth over scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and integration of the Chorus
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chorus too should be regarded as one of the actors; it should be an integral part of the whole, and share in the action, in the manner not of Euripides but of Sophocles. The choral songs of later poets are often mere interludes and unrelated to the piece.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the Chorus a participant in the plot and thematically connected to the action; avoid choral interludes that interrupt unity or could belong to any play. Keep the chorus tied structurally and emotionally to the drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid irrational elements within the action
rubrics_metrics.description: Within the action there must be nothing irrational. If the irrational cannot be excluded, it should be outside the scope of the tragedy (as with the irrational element in Sophocles' Oedipus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep events and causes intelligible to the audience. If you must include miraculous or irrational items, present them as preconditions or consequences outside the action’s internal causality so they do not undermine dramatic plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staging vividness: visualize scene and gestures
rubrics_metrics.description: In constructing the plot and working it out with the help of language, the poet should place the scene, as far as possible, before his eyes. Seeing everything with the utmost vividness, as if he were a spectator of the action, he will discover what is in keeping with it, and be most unlikely to overlook inconsistencies. The poet should work out his play with appropriate gestures; those who feel emotion are most impressive by force of sympathy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose with strong visual imagination: picture settings, actions, and gestures. Use stageable, vivid details and gestures that elicit sympathy—this reduces inconsistency and heightens dramatic effect. Avoid referencing actions the audience cannot plausibly perceive without explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language and Thought (dianoia): purpose of speeches
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Thought is included every effect which has to be produced by speech; in particular—proof and refutation; the excitation of feelings (pity, fear, anger); the heightening or extenuating of facts. Dramatic incidents must be treated from the same points of view as the dramatic speeches when the object is to evoke pity, fear, grandeur, or probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design speeches to accomplish rhetorical ends—establish proofs, refute accusations, and rouse or temper emotions appropriately. Align verbal strategies with the intended emotional impact on the audience; where incidents already display the fact, speeches should not merely restate them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction and figures: familiarity with speech acts and metre
rubrics_metrics.description: As regards Diction, know the Figures of Speech and the elements of declamation—what is a command, prayer, narrative, threat, question, answer—also letters, syllables, connecting words, nouns, verbs, inflexions, and how these relate to metre and vocal quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be competent in rhetorical forms and in the components of language that affect meter and diction. Though some fine points belong to declaimers, the poet who ignores these risks faults in expression and metre; attend to sentence types, figures, and phonetic/meter considerations when composing lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design process: sketch general outline then fill episodes
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet, whether he accepts traditional subjects or invents new ones, should, in shaping them himself, first sketch the general outline of the play, and then fill in the episodes and amplify in detail. Sketch the general plan of the play, and then fill in the episodes, making them appropriate and of right length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with an overall scheme of beginning, reversal, and ending; then craft episodes that serve that scheme. Avoid improvising episodes that do not cohere with the general plan; ensure order and proportionality (short episodes in drama).

rubrics_metrics.name: Propriety of traits to roles (gender/role appropriateness)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a type of manly valour; but for a woman to be valiant in the same sense, or terrible, would be inappropriate. Character traits should be fitting to the person’s class and role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign traits to characters consistent with their social/gender/role expectations unless a deliberate and consistently handled inversion is intended. Avoid incongruous portrayals (example: male types or lament tones that do not suit the character).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of character (even if originally inconsistent)
rubrics_metrics.description: The fourth point is consistency: for even though the original character, who suggested the type, be inconsistent, still he must be consistently inconsistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a character has contradictory tendencies, present those contradictions in a stable, recognisable pattern so the audience perceives consistent motivation rather than arbitrary shifts (example: Iphigenia at Aulis appearing differently in different scenes is a fault).
